content: US Defense CEO Fired Again Over Sex Scandal. His First Was on a Private Jet Chris Kubasik holds a dubious distinction in the defense industry. He’s been forced out of two CEO roles over personal misconduct. Strike One (2012): As Lockheed Martin’s CEO-elect, weeks from taking the top job, he was busted for a sexual relationship with a subordinate. Reports say he was caught in the act on a company jet. He was forced to resign immediately but still pocketed $3.5 million in severance. His downfall landed on the same day CIA Director Petraeus resigned over his own affair. Strike Two (2026): Somehow, the defense industry gave him another shot. He climbed back to become chairman and CEO of L3Harris Technologies, one of the largest defense contractors in the US. On August 17, 2026, they forced him out again for conduct “not consistent with company values.” This time the board showed no mercy: zero severance, zero benefits, no golden parachute. The company won’t specify what happened, but the pattern is hard to miss. Same man. Same type of scandal. Two of America’s biggest defense companies. Fourteen years apart. Source: Clash Report

Ukraine's population has dropped 45% since independence — from 52 million to around 29 million living on Kyiv-controlled territory. Nearly 7 million are refugees abroad, and the number wanting to return has fallen below 50% for the first time. The country loses an estimated 100,000-150,000 people monthly to long-term emigration — far more than battlefield casualties. Birth rates have hit a record low of 0.9 children per woman, with deaths nearly three times higher than births. As one demographer put it: There will never be 52 million of us again. We need to plan around 30 million. Source: RFE/RL
The U.S. has lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones—about 25% of its fleet—during the Iran war, with losses costing more than $1.3 billion. Source: WaPo

The Iranian Army officially announces that 3 out of 4 Su-24 pilots ejected safely after returning from a bombing raid on Doha in March, and are still alive being held by Qatar after 5 months The pilots Javad Salehi, Abdul Majid Dashtian, and Omran Behrushian, were captured alive after their jets were downed by air defenses on the way back to Iran, after they successfully bombed a U.S. base. The Iranian Army demands the immediate adherence to the Geneva Conventions, sections 70 and 78, which should allow the prisoners to contact the Red Cross, their own families, and inform them their current condition.
